text: Museum curators treat the intent to deceive as central to fakes and forgeries; the motives of makers and sellers vary — money, frustration that their own work is unappreciated, a wish to fool the experts, or a need for attention.
When an artist's work reaches high prices at auction, or a major study of an artist is published, many previously unknown works may suddenly appear on the market.

Attributions carry degrees of certainty: 'by' an artist shows reasonable certainty; 'attributed to' signals some doubt; 'studio of' means a pupil, probably under the master's direction; a 'follower' admired the style without necessarily being a pupil; an 'imitator' may have worked much later.
An autograph painting is one thought to have been painted entirely by the named artist, rather than partly or wholly by studio assistants.
Medieval and Renaissance painters worked in workshops with apprentices and assistants; a painting made by the chief assistant without the master's participation is called a workshop piece.

The Getty Museum dates its marble kouros 'about 530 B.C. or modern forgery' and states that neither art historians nor scientists have been able to completely resolve the question of its authenticity.

The Getty lists the doubts — a mixture of earlier and later stylistic traits and the use of marble from Thasos at an unexpected date — but suggests the anomalies may reflect limited knowledge of Greek sculpture of the period rather than a forger's mistakes.
note: This is the owning museum's own reading. Its catalogue date ('about 530 B.C. or modern forgery') shows the attribution remains unresolved, and the anomalies it lists are the reasons many doubt the statue.

text: Since prison, John Myatt sells 'genuine fakes': each work is clearly signed so that it can never be sold as authentic.

For about thirty years Mark Landis gave fakes to dozens of museums and university galleries while posing as a philanthropist; because the institutions lost no money and he claimed no tax deductions, he technically committed no fraud.

Landis aged works with coffee or brown pigment, used cheap craft-store materials and forged labels; under a microscope one of his paintings showed printed pixels — he glued a printout of a digital image to board, sanded it and painted over it.
A staff member at the Oklahoma City Museum of Art spotted the pattern of odd donations; after media attention Landis stopped donating to museums in 2014.

Giovanni Morelli (1816–1891) developed a method of connoisseurship that attributes paintings through minute, habitual details of an artist's hand; he published it under the pseudonym Ivan Lermolieff, in articles from the 1870s and a book in 1880.
Morelli's approach was taken up by the next generation of connoisseurs, including Bernard Berenson.
Impasto is paint built up thickly so that brush or palette-knife marks show and catch the light — used for highlights by Rembrandt and extensively by Van Gogh.
A glaze is a transparent or translucent paint film laid over a usually lighter colour; it modifies the colour beneath without hiding it.

A pentimento is a change the artist made while painting, usually hidden under later paint; pentimenti can be detected with infrared reflectograms and X-rays and are sometimes helpful in attributing paintings.
'Renaissance' (rebirth) names the revival of interest in the art and culture of Antiquity in Italy from the 14th century; as a period it broadly runs from the 15th century to the end of the 16th.
'Baroque' usefully describes large, usually 17th-century works that are dramatic and exuberant, with diagonal compositions and illusionistic effects — Rubens and Bernini are typical examples.
Rococo is the style of painting and decoration popular in France under Louis XV (1715–1774): asymmetry, curved forms and light, bright colours.
Realism, in its specific sense, was a mid-19th-century movement painting everyday life in a naturalistic manner.

The name Impressionism came from a painting by Monet exhibited independently of the Paris Salon in 1874; the group exhibited together eight times up to 1886, working rapidly, often outdoors, and using new artists' materials.
Post-impressionism describes developments from about 1886, usually confined to Cézanne, Gauguin, Seurat and Van Gogh.
Cubism was invented around 1907–08 by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, combining different views of a subject in one picture.
Abstract expressionism was developed by American painters such as Jackson Pollock, Mark Rothko and Willem de Kooning in the 1940s and 1950s.
Pop art emerged in the 1950s and flourished in the 1960s in America and Britain, drawing on popular and commercial culture.
Jackson Pollock (1912–1956) is best known for the drip paintings he made between 1947 and 1950.
Paint is pigment — the source of colour — mixed with a medium that binds it; media include egg tempera, watercolour, oil and glue size.
Egg tempera uses egg yolk as the medium; it has been used since Antiquity, most early Italian paintings are in it, and it became less common after 1500.

Oil paint was used in Northern Europe in the 13th and 14th centuries; innovations by Van Eyck and Campin reached Italy in the early 15th century. It dries slowly and is more flexible than egg tempera.

Canvas — usually hemp or flax stretched over a wooden frame — became a common support; the earliest surviving painted canvases date from the late 14th century, and wooden panels were previously the most common support.
A ground layer prepares the support; on panels it is usually gesso — gypsum bound in animal-skin size — applied coarse then fine and sanded absolutely smooth.
An underdrawing is the preliminary outline of the composition on the primed support; infrared imaging can reveal it.
Varnish gives a painting gloss and protection; waxes, tree and fossil resins, oil–resin mixtures and synthetics have all been used, and varnishes tend to darken and discolour over time.
Craquelure is the network of cracks that develops as paint layers age and shrink; most old pictures show it everywhere, usually extending into the varnish.
A paint cross-section is a minute sample mounted in resin and polished; under the microscope it shows the layer structure and the pigments used, which helps date a picture.
Lead white (basic lead carbonate) was the main white pigment used by artists until the 19th century.
Natural ultramarine, the richest and most expensive blue, was made from lapis lazuli mined in Badakhshan in Afghanistan; an artificial form, French Ultramarine, was discovered in the 19th century.
Vermilion is an ancient red pigment, used by painters long before the modern era.
Prussian blue, the oldest modern synthetic pigment, has been in use since its discovery in 1704.
Cobalt blue is a 19th-century pigment, not commercially manufactured until the early 1800s, so its presence gives a terminus post quem in the 19th century.
Emerald green has been in use since its discovery in the first quarter of the 19th century; it was discontinued in the second half of the 20th century because of its extreme toxicity.
Chromium was discovered in 1797, and chrome yellow has been used as a pigment since the first quarter of the 19th century.
Zinc white only became available to artists in the early 19th century.
Cadmium pigments have been in use since about 1840.
Titanium white was first produced in Norway in 1918 and in the United States a year later; it was first sold as an artists' paint in 1920 in the USA and by 1924 in Europe.

Exact pigment introduction dates are often disputed: one standard reference puts the first commercial artists' titanium white in Europe in 1919, with only limited experimental availability before 1916.

In a survey of 184 paintings made between 1920 and the 1990s, titanium white turned up in only sixteen; in the first half of the 20th century it was extremely rare, appearing on palettes only towards the 1940s.
Phthalocyanine pigments were developed around the 1930s.
Acrylic-styrene-acrylonitrile (ASA) terpolymers, found in the paint of fake 'Pollocks', have been commercially available only since 1970.

Materials typical of the 20th century (such as titanium white or cadmium red) or of the 19th century (such as zinc white, cobalt blue, cadmium yellow or chromium pigments) give a terminus post quem for an artwork.

The terminus post quem — the earliest possible date of a painting — comes from comparing its materials with their earliest dates of discovery or production; it gives relative information only and may fail to prove a forgery.

X-ray fluorescence (XRF) identifies chemical elements, not compounds, so pigment identification is a deduction: a red containing mercury is most likely cinnabar or vermilion, but other reds — perhaps from a restoration or a forgery — cannot be ruled out.
Portable XRF cannot identify individual light elements, organic compounds almost completely elude it, and a single-point reading cannot tell which layer an element sits in.
Portable XRF is the dominant non-destructive method in authentication, but its misuse is documented and widespread; results must be interpreted for the instrument used and not over-interpreted.
Raman spectroscopy can distinguish compounds unambiguously at high spatial resolution, so combining it (and other methods) with XRF is often essential.
In one case study, XRF detected cobalt but could not tell smalt, an old pigment, from modern cobalt blue.
X-ray and UV photography and chemical analysis of pigments entered art authentication in the 1930s.
Under ultraviolet light, traditional natural resin varnishes glow a characteristic greenish yellow; retouchings applied on top of the varnish block the UV and show as dark patches.
Infrared radiation passes through paint layers until something absorbs it; carbon black absorbs strongly, so an underdrawing in black on a white ground shows up in an infrared image.
Heavier atoms block X-rays more, so pigments containing lead or mercury, and the nails in a support, show up white in an X-radiograph; losses show dark, and all layers appear superimposed.
Lead has atomic number 82 and is a heavy metal present in lead white.

A 3D imaging study comparing original cracks with cracks forged by an expert found original cracks roughly rectangular in section and as deep as the upper layer, while the fakes were simpler V-shaped grooves.
Forgery researchers describe craquelure as one of the most difficult features of old paintings to mimic convincingly.
note: Stated in a 2026 preprint that had not been peer reviewed when checked; the 3D study (kim-2022) supports the narrower point that forged cracks differ in shape.

text: Vasari reports that Michelangelo carved a life-size sleeping Cupid, that Lorenzo di Pier Francesco de' Medici told him it would pass for an antique if buried and made to look old, and — in one version — that it was sold in Rome to Cardinal San Giorgio as an antique for 200 ducats.

Vasari also records a version in which the dealer told Michelangelo the Cupid had fetched only 30 crowns, and the Cardinal, learning it had been made in Florence, forced the dealer's agent to return the money.

Cornelis Hofstede de Groot, a leading expert on Dutch painting, accepted the 'Laughing Cavalier' (c. 1923) as a Frans Hals in The Burlington Magazine; it was soon shown to contain modern nails and pigments, yet he stood by his attribution.

Hofstede de Groot also bought 'Amused smoker' in 1923 as a Hals and kept defending it after it was declared a forgery for containing water-soluble paint; its attribution to Van Meegeren is not certain.

The 1925 court case over the Laughing Cavalier was the first time chemical and technical evidence was used in a Dutch court to expose a forged painting; the experts reported artificial ultramarine, cobalt blue, zinc white and machine-made nails.
note: The RKD confirms modern nails and pigments; the 'first time' claim and the specific pigment list come from a 2026 preprint (based on the court archive) that had not been peer reviewed when checked.

text: The lawsuit was halted before a verdict when Hofstede de Groot bought the painting for the full 50,000 guilders; he then argued in print that his expert eye should outweigh the chemical evidence.
note: The book's title and subject are confirmed by a library record; the purchase and its framing rest on a 2026 preprint that had not been peer reviewed when checked.

text: In 1925 Hofstede de Groot published 'Echt of onecht? Oog of chemie?' — 'Real or fake? The eye or chemistry?' — about the court case.

The Laughing Cavalier resurfaced in 2024 and is being re-examined at the start of ARTDETECT, a European Research Council project that will systematically analyse painted forgeries and test methods for detecting them.
note: Reported in a 2026 preprint by the project team, not yet peer reviewed when checked.

text: 'The Supper at Emmaus', discovered in 1937, was hailed by Dutch art historians as Vermeer's masterpiece and compared in importance to Rembrandt's Night Watch; Museum Boijmans' director beat the Rijksmuseum to it for 520,000 guilders.
Museum Boijmans now catalogues 'The Supper at Emmaus' as painted in 1937 by the forger Han van Meegeren (1889–1947), and keeps four of his paintings.
The Rijksmuseum paid 1.3 million guilders for Van Meegeren's 'Washing of the Feet'; a contemporary curator wrote in his diary that it was 'bad and crude' and absurd to attribute to Vermeer.

When Van Meegeren's 1942 'Christ and the Adulteress', sold as a Vermeer, was found in Hermann Göring's collection, Van Meegeren was arrested for collaborating with the Nazis by selling Dutch heritage — a charge punishable by death — and confessed that he had painted it.
To prove his confession, Van Meegeren painted a new work in Vermeer's style.
The charge was changed from collaboration to forgery; Van Meegeren was convicted of forgery and fraud, sentenced to one year in prison, and died in 1947 before serving it.

Van Meegeren used Bakelite, an early plastic, to harden his paint so that it passed the period's age tests — an alcohol swab and a heated needle; Bakelite is now readily identified by instrumental analysis.
The phenol-formaldehyde resin (Bakelite) in Van Meegeren's paint was identified by UV spectroscopy in 1956, according to papers in the ICCROM archives.
A copy of Dirck van Baburen's 'The Procuress' at the Courtauld showed no modern pigments in 2009, but later analysis found Bakelite and it was confirmed as Van Meegeren's in 2011.
Analysis published in 2011 showed that Van Meegeren's paint also contained pigments not introduced until the 19th century.
Van Meegeren scraped the paint off old paintings to reuse their canvases, giving his fakes a naturally aged support; Wolfgang Beltracchi bought frames and supports at antique markets.

A 1967 study showed that old and modern lead can be told apart by measuring lead-210, which decays with a 22-year half-life once it is separated from its long-lived parent radium-226 when lead is refined from ore.

Elmyr de Hory (1906–1976) posed as a dispossessed Hungarian aristocrat; with the dealer Fernand Legros he sold forgeries on five continents over nine years, until they were unmasked in 1967 after 40 paintings sold to the Texas collector Algur Meadows were identified as fakes.

De Hory bought 19th-century paintings at Paris flea markets and scraped them down to the primer before painting; Legros copied experts' certification stamps and inserted photographs of the forgeries into auction catalogues and monographs.

John Drewe posed as a wealthy collector to get into museum archives, then stole, altered and added documents to support John Myatt's fakes; after a Scotland Yard investigation and a 1999 trial, Myatt received one year and Drewe six.
Myatt often used household paint — mixed with lubricating jelly to mimic oil — and rubbed canvases with coffee grounds and vacuum-cleaner dust to age them.
Myatt was convicted over more than 200 forged modernist paintings made over seven years; about 120 are thought to still be circulating.

Shaun Greenhalgh made several hundred forgeries; his 'Amarna Princess' was acquired by Bolton Council after a British Museum report authenticated it as 3,300 years old. He was released from prison in 2010, and the statue is now displayed in Bolton Museum.

Robert Trotter stripped old, low-value paintings, repainted and artificially aged them and invented provenances; he admitted selling 52 paintings to six dealers, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and was sentenced to ten months in prison.

The court ordered Trotter's forgeries to be indelibly stamped as forgeries before return, and gave some to Yale University Art Gallery and Buffalo State College to help identify his work still in circulation.

From 1994 to 2009 the dealer Glafira Rosales sold more than 60 never-exhibited works attributed to artists such as Pollock, Rothko and Motherwell to two Manhattan galleries for about $33.2 million; the galleries resold them for more than $80 million.
Rosales' provenance was invented: an anonymous Swiss client who never existed and a Spanish collector who never owned the works; an accomplice gave the paintings a false patina of age.
Rosales pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court in September 2013 to charges including wire fraud and money laundering, and agreed to forfeit $33.2 million.

Knoedler & Company, one of New York's oldest and most reputable galleries, closed in 2011 after being accused of selling forged Abstract Expressionist paintings — all painted by one man, Pei-Shen Qian, in Queens.

Buyers argued that the number of works, the huge profit margins and the mysterious provenance were red flags the gallery ignored; the gallery's director said experts she consulted believed the works genuine.
Beltracchi recreated works that were recorded in old catalogues but had no surviving pictures or had been lost in the war — he 'filled the gap'.

Tells in Beltracchi's fakes included woodworm holes drilled with a drill, artificial patina, unprimed tacking margins where Campendonk used pre-primed linen, and labels documenting a fictitious Flechtheim collection.
On 29 November 2006 a Cologne auction house sold 'Red Picture with Horses', signed 'Campendonk 1914', for €2.4 million plus fees — €2.88 million in all — against an estimate of €0.8–1.2 million.

Campendonk's catalogue raisonné listed a painting of that title, exhibited at Galerie Flechtheim in 1920. The forgery came with an invented family collection and a 'Sammlung Flechtheim' label — but there was no evidence the Flechtheim collection had ever used such a label.
The court found the auction house had neither checked the consignor's provenance nor had the painting scientifically examined before the sale.
In March 2008 the Doerner Institut found titanium white in its rutile form in two layers of the 'Campendonk' — a pigment industrially produced only from 1937/38.
In 2011 a Cologne court sentenced Wolfgang Beltracchi to six years in prison.

On 9 October 2026 Germany's Federal Court of Justice heard the forger's claim to get 'Red Picture with Horses' back after the sale was unwound and the painting resold; lower courts had rejected the claim and a ruling is scheduled for January.
note: The court's own listing gives the ruling date as '15 January 2026', which precedes the hearing; January 2027 is evidently meant. Legal press reported that the court indicated the appeal was unlikely to succeed.

text: Between 2005 and 2014 John Re sold dozens of fake Pollocks and de Koonings with a story about a basement cache; IFAR found no evidence for it, and in November 2014 he pleaded guilty to wire fraud and admitted fabricating the provenance.

In 2023 Michael Barzman admitted that he and another man made fake Basquiats on cardboard in 2012 — sometimes in as little as five minutes each — and invented a provenance from a famous screenwriter's storage unit; the works became an exhibition at the Orlando Museum of Art in February 2022, and the FBI seized 25 pieces in June 2022.
On the back of one seized painting, Barzman's own name appeared on a mailing label that had been painted over.

XRF can date silver: metal refined before the mid-19th century contains traces of gold and lead, so their absence shows silver refined after about 1850. A collector who bought nearly 280 objects from two Philadelphia dealers found that 90% of the fakes in his collection came from them.

Dendrochronology dates a wooden panel by matching its sequence of ring widths to a regional master chronology; it works for oak but not for poplar, the usual wood of Italian panels, whose growth is too erratic.
Panel makers cut away the bark and sapwood, so a panel's youngest ring is not the felling date; the missing sapwood rings have to be estimated statistically.

Baltic oak, the usual wood of Netherlandish panels, has a minimum of 9, a median of 15 and a maximum of 36 sapwood rings (half of trees 13–19); oak from Germany or the Netherlands has a median of 17 (half 13–23) and a minimum of 7.
For most 16th- and 17th-century oak panels, two to eight years passed between felling and painting; 15th-century panels suggest an average of ten to fifteen years.

Worked example: a panel whose youngest ring is 1466 gives an earliest felling date of 1475 (9 sapwood rings) and a median of 1481 (15 rings); with ten years' seasoning, a painting date from 1491 onward is plausible.
Worked example: a youngest ring of 1603 implies an earliest felling date of 1612 and, with the median sapwood count and two years' seasoning, a plausible painting date from 1620.
The National Gallery bought 'A Man with a Skull' in 1845 as a Holbein; analysis of its wooden panel showed the work postdates Holbein's death.
A painting the National Gallery acquired in 1923 as a 15th-century work was proven by scientific analysis of its materials to be a 20th-century forgery.

Radiocarbon dating of a Trotter forgery signed 'Sarah Honn, May 5, 1866' found the canvas consistent with that date, but the oil binding the paint came from seeds harvested in 1958–1961 or 1983–1989; Trotter had confessed to painting it in 1985.
That result needed a paint sample of 160 micrograms, of which about 19 micrograms of carbon remained for measurement after cleaning.
Nuclear weapons testing sharply raised atmospheric carbon-14 between 1954 and 1963; it has declined since, which is why a single post-1950 measurement can match two calendar ranges.
In the northern-hemisphere record, the annual mean F14C of the air rose from 0.974 in 1950 to 1.90 in 1964 — nearly double — and fell back to 1.01 by 2019.
note: Computed from the annual NH zone 1 compilation (14C ages converted with F = exp(−age/8033)); the mid-year values are 1950.5, 1964.5 and 2019.5.

text: A canvas's radiocarbon date reflects when its fibres were harvested; a lag of two to five years between that date and the date on the work is not uncommon.

Lead isotopes in the lead white of 77 well-dated paintings by 27 Dutch artists shifted at the start, middle and end of the 17th century, tracking events such as the English Civil War — a possible new tool for dating and authentication.

Provenance is the history of a work's ownership, pieced together from descriptions, collection inventories, inventory numbers on the work itself and auction catalogues; the National Gallery pays particular attention to where its paintings were between 1933 and 1945.
On 3 December 1998, 44 states endorsed the non-binding Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-confiscated art, starting with the duty to identify confiscated art never restituted.
For the principles' 25th anniversary, 'Best Practices' clarifying how to apply them were presented on 5 March 2024.
INTERPOL launched its free ID-Art app on 6 May 2021, giving anyone mobile access to its database of stolen works of art — then more than 52,000 items, now almost 57,000.
The final volume of the Rembrandt Research Project's Corpus (2014), by Ernst van de Wetering, opens with two chapters: 'What is a Rembrandt?' and 'What is a non-Rembrandt?'.
Authentication experts in court are often pressed to answer 'authentic or not' in simple yes-or-no terms, although the evidence usually supports only degrees of probability.
In 2018 researchers presented automated, stroke-level analysis of drawings by artists such as Picasso and Matisse for attribution and authentication.

A 2024 peer-reviewed study used transfer learning on multi-scale image tiles to separate authentic from imitation Pollock poured paintings with 98.9% accuracy, noting that the small number of available images is a limitation.

Because few known forgeries exist to train on, a 2024 study added AI-generated images in an artist's style to training sets and found they consistently improved detection of human-made forgeries of Van Gogh, Modigliani and Raphael.
A 2021 study trained a decision-support model on 55 examined artworks, 12 of them forged, and concluded that much larger datasets of works with known provenance are needed.

The Swiss company Art Recognition analyses high-resolution photographs with artist-specific AI models and gives a yes-or-no assessment of stylistic consistency, issuing a certificate of authenticity if positive; it excludes sculpture, drip painting and street art.
Art Recognition says the first auction house to offer a work on the strength of its certificate alone was Germann Auctions in Zurich, in November 2024.

Art Recognition says some artists have fewer than 50 authenticated works to train on, and that it enlarges such datasets by augmentation, including synthetic examples generated in the model's latent space.

In 2021 an Art Recognition analysis, publicised by the company and the press, judged the National Gallery's 'Samson and Delilah' about 91% likely not to be by Rubens; the Gallery continues to catalogue it as Rubens, about 1609–10.
note: An AI result from a photograph; the 91% figure is as reported by The Guardian/Observer and publicised on the company's site. The owning museum maintains the attribution to Rubens; no peer-reviewed publication of the analysis was found.

text: In January 2023 the University of Bradford announced, ahead of a peer-reviewed paper, that facial-recognition software found the faces in the de Brécy Tondo 'identical' to those in Raphael's Sistine Madonna and that the works were 'undoubtedly by the same artist'.
Art Recognition's model then classified the de Brécy Tondo as not by Raphael with 85% probability; a second Bradford model, trained on 49 images, again returned 'authentic'.
note: Reported by Art Recognition, itself a party to the dispute. The two AI results contradict each other; the attribution remains unresolved.

text: Facial similarity is weak evidence of authorship: Renaissance painters worked within shared ideals of beauty, so resembling faces may reflect the period rather than the hand.
note: Argued by a competitor of the Bradford team; reasonable, but made by an interested party.

text: The National Gallery's 2010 exhibition 'Close Examination: Fakes, Mistakes and Discoveries' showed how scientific examination, conservation and art-historical research together uncover workshop pieces, period copies and modern forgeries.

Two of the six authors of the 2024 synthetic-images study are affiliated with Art Recognition AG, including its chief executive and co-founder, Carina Popovici; the paper declares no competing interests.

In September 2012 the Cologne Regional Court ordered the auction house — which had itself been deceived and acted in good faith — to pay the buyer €2,086,080 plus interest against return of the painting, because its catalogue had presented the attribution to Campendonk as certain without a sufficient factual basis.
